question: What is the primary design purpose of data hiding (encapsulation) in object-oriented programming?

options.text: To protect internal invariants and isolate implementation details from external callers.
To make private fields functionally identical to public fields through getter access.
To prevent instances of the same class from reading private fields of each other.
To encrypt data in heap memory so operating system processes cannot inspect variable values.

explanation: Data hiding protects object integrity by ensuring state can only be accessed or modified through controlled methods that enforce invariants.

question: Why is declaring a mutable reference field as `public final Date timestamp;` insufficient for data hiding?

options.text: Public final fields are encrypted by the classloader and cannot be inspected at runtime.
The final modifier automatically changes field access to private in bytecode compilation.
The compiler forbids declaring public final fields on mutable reference types in Java classes.
Callers cannot reassign timestamp, but can still mutate the internal state of the referenced Date object.

explanation: Making a reference final prevents reassigning the reference variable itself, but does not prevent external callers from mutating the underlying object's state.

question: How is the `private` access boundary enforced in the Java language?

options.text: Per-thread: only the specific thread that constructed the instance can read its private state.
Per-package: all classes within the same package can freely inspect private fields.
Per-object: one instance of a class cannot access private fields of another instance of the same class.
Per-class: code within the class can access private members of any instance of that same class.

explanation: Privacy in Java is class-based, not object-based; any method in class C can access private fields of any instance of class C.

question: How does providing a getter method without a corresponding setter method support encapsulation?

options.text: It makes the field functionally equivalent to a public field without any restrictions.
It grants read-only access while preventing outside classes from modifying the internal field directly.
It eliminates the requirement to declare the field with private access modifier.
It encrypts the returned value so external callers cannot read its primitive value.

explanation: Omitting a setter prevents external code from mutating the field, establishing a read-only property and preserving invariants.
